title: President pledges investment protection, opens major projects to private sector | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:04
-     - 328

By Charumini de Silva

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake yesterday pledged stronger safeguards for investors and greater private-sector participation in infrastructure and economic development.

He made this pledge outlining a series of proposed changes spanning ports, logistics, energy, taxation, and technology at the inauguration of the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026 organised by The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce.

Addressing a packed business audience during a Fireside Chat moderated by Standard Chartered Bank Sri Lanka CEO and Ceylon Chamber Vice Chairperson Bingumal Thewarathanthri, the President stressed that investment protection, transparency, predictable rules, and infrastructure development must be matched by stronger domestic businesses capable of partnering with foreign investors.

“If there are not strong local entrepreneurs and businesses, with whom can the foreign investors do businesses or joint ventures?” he asked, urging the private sector to play a more active role in expanding the economy.

He said the Government would consider extending tax concessions to businesses investing in rural areas to create new economic opportunities, while also signalling a review of existing fuel-sector agreements and a shift towards competitive procurement and pricing mechanisms in selected areas.

Among the most significant announcements was the Government’s intention to offer management and operating rights of the East Container Terminal (ECT) at Port of Colombo to a private-sector partner while retaining State ownership. The terminal is currently operated by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA).

The President said the Terminal’s current throughput was approximately 500,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs), compared with a potential annual capacity of 3.2 million TEUs once fully developed and optimised.

He argued that delays in port operations meant the country was not making the best use of its existing assets, highlighting the opportunity for international terminal operators and shipping lines to improve efficiency and expand capacity.

Industry reports indicate that five to six international shipping lines have expressed interest, although the Government has yet to formally identify a preferred operator or announce the terms and timeline of the proposed arrangement.

The move could reshape competition among Colombo’s container terminals and influence the Port’s transshipment business, provided the eventual operating structure delivers the anticipated capacity and efficiency gains.

The Government is also pursuing a substantial expansion of port infrastructure. The President said approximately $ 1.4 billion would be required for breakwater infrastructure supporting the proposed West Container Terminal II (WCT II).

Financing is expected to be sought from multilateral development institutions. Preliminary design-related work has progressed with support from the Asian Development Bank (ADB), with the final report expected by April 2027, according to the President.

WCT II is expected to add around 3.2 million TEUs in annual capacity upon completion, creating further opportunities for terminal operators, maritime service providers, and other port-related investors.

The SLPA also intends to call a fresh tender for a logistics centre within Port of Colombo after a dispute involving land previously allocated to other parties was resolved, the President said. Compensation is to be paid to the previous parties, after which the land is expected to be released for the new tender.

The proposed development could attract investment into bonded warehousing, container freight stations, distribution, cargo consolidation, and value-added logistics services.

Separately, the Government plans to establish a container examination facility in Kerawalapitiya through a public-private partnership (PPP). The President referred to a facility capable of examining approximately 150 containers, although further details on its operational capacity and implementation timeline were not provided.

The project, which has received Cabinet approval for a PPP-based approach, is intended to ease congestion, improve Customs clearance, and increase cargo-handling efficiency.

The Government is considering reducing the existing 2.5% tax or levy affecting bunkering through the Budget 2027, following representations from the Bunkering Committee, the President said.

He said the objective was to strengthen Sri Lanka’s competitiveness as a regional bunkering centre, with the Government also considering a partnership between the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) and private-sector operators to expand bunker-fuel storage at the JCT Oil Bank.

The President also announced plans to establish 75 additional CPC filling stations, while confirming that existing agreements with Lanka IOC, Sinopec, and other private fuel suppliers would be reviewed with the involvement of the Attorney General.

He expressed concern that current arrangements could constrain the Government’s ability to respond to international oil-price volatility and supply disruptions, particularly where private operators limit distribution despite having stocks.

“Although in urban areas both public and private fuel stations are available, in outstations only one player is available and mostly private sheds. Limiting distribution by private players due to price while having stocks is not correct and fair,” he said.

The Government wants to strengthen its capacity to ensure uninterrupted domestic fuel availability, while expecting private operators to balance commercial returns with their wider responsibilities.

“Be a competitive player. Profit and social responsibility is something that the private sector must consider,” the President said.

The proposed review follows broader concerns about the flexibility of existing fuel-market arrangements and the State’s ability to maintain supplies during periods of disruption.

The President said renewable energy development would continue in collaboration with the private sector, with four grid lines expected to be opened for private-sector participation.

He questioned the reliance on fixed feed-in tariffs, noting that rates are determined by the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL), and argued that competitive tendering would help bring down costs.

He also identified land scarcity as a constraint on solar development, suggesting that greater emphasis would be placed on floating solar parks, citing the recent Ibbankatuwa project as an example.

The proposed approach would seek to expand renewable energy capacity while addressing land limitations and improving cost competitiveness.

The President said the Government had managed to secure uninterrupted supplies of oil, gas, and fuel amid escalating tensions in the Middle East, but cautioned that the future course of the conflict remained uncertain.

He said the Government had allocated Rs. 60 billion in fuel concessions to cushion the economy against another shock following the economic crisis and Cyclone Ditwah, and had extended relief through a further Rs. 41 billion allocation for targeted communities.

Identifying eligible beneficiaries remains a challenge because of gaps in available data, he said, adding that Mobitel and Dialog were discussing possible solutions.

The President identified workforce skills and productivity as critical to Sri Lanka’s ability to attract investment, particularly in information and communications technology (ICT), where industry requirements have evolved rapidly.

He said the Government planned to sign an agreement with Singapore next week to establish a training centre on Wijerama Mawatha, aimed at strengthening capacity in ICT and artificial intelligence (AI). The proposal is also expected to be submitted for Cabinet approval next week.

Sri Lanka needed to develop its IT skills beyond current levels to match the requirements of a changing global market, he said, while pointing to the need to improve salary structures in the public sector and specialised fields to attract and retain expertise.

title: President keeps door open to fresh IMF deal | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:07
-     - 142

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake yesterday said Sri Lanka was open to entering a fresh International Monetary Fund (IMF) program after its current arrangement ends, but stressed that no decision had been taken as the Government weighs growth ambitions against the need to preserve economic stability.

President keeps...

Speaking during a fireside chat at the inauguration of the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026, organised by the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, the President said discussions were underway on the possibility of a new agreement that would shift the focus from crisis recovery towards economic growth without reversing the gains made under the existing IMF-backed program.

“We are at a mid-level and open about it,” he said, adding that the Government would use the remaining six months of the current arrangement to assess its options before determining the future of its engagement with the Fund.

The President said Sri Lanka had made considerable progress in restoring economic stability with improved international ratings, but foreign exchange reserves still needed to reach the desired level and the country’s credit standing required further improvement.

Any decision on a successor program would depend on the state of the economy, the strength of reserves and the extent to which Sri Lanka could withstand further external shocks amid heightened global uncertainty.

Dissanayake warned that Sri Lanka’s fuel import expenditure could rise to around $ 6 billion in 2026 if current trends continued. “In 2025, the fuel import bill for the year was over $ 4.04 billion ($ 4,042 million) and during the first eight months of 2026 it has reached over $ 4.08 billion ($ 4,082 million),” he said, highlighting the potential impact of the Middle East conflict on the country’s external position.

The projected increase would place additional pressure on foreign exchange requirements at a time when the Government is seeking to consolidate the recovery and strengthen its external buffers.

The President said the evolving international situation was among the factors that would shape the Government’s assessment of whether the economy could withstand further shocks without additional support.

However he did not indicate that a new IMF program was inevitable, though his remarks suggest that the decision will be influenced by the resilience of the recovery and the country’s capacity to manage external risks.

The President said the existing IMF program had primarily focused on restoring economic stability following the crisis, while a possible successor arrangement should give greater weight to growth.

“We are examining what form such an agreement could take, with senior economic officials, including representatives of the Finance Ministry and the Central Bank, involved in discussions,” he added.

He said the administration would be prepared to enter into another agreement if it could reach an understanding with the IMF that supported Sri Lanka’s economic growth objectives.

However, he reiterated that the Government had neither decided to end its engagement with the Fund nor committed itself to a fresh program.

The President also defended the Government’s cooperation with the IMF, noting there had been relatively few contradictions between the administration’s economic objectives and the commitments under the current program. “This has enabled implementation to continue without major disagreements,” he stressed.

Sri Lanka has entered into or sought IMF support on 17 occasions since joining the institution. Its current arrangement is a 48-month Extended Fund Facility (EFF) approved on 20 March 2023, with financing of approximately $ 3 billion, equivalent to SDR 2.286 billion. The program is scheduled to run until 19 March 2027.

title: Sri Lanka qualify for final with Bangladesh | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:21
-     - 15

Limansa Thilakarathna ran through the Pakistan middle order taking three wickets, Sanjana Kavindi was once again top scorer for Sri Lanka with 46

Sri Lanka secured their fourth win in the ongoing Pakistan Women’s Under19 T20 Tri-Series to qualify for the final with a game in hand when they beat the hosts Pakistan by six wickets at Faisalabad yesterday.

It was Sri Lanka’s third win on the trot after they lost their first match of the Tri-Series to Pakistan by five wickets.

Pakistan batting first were kept down to a total of 105-8 by the right-arm slow medium deliveries of Yeshali Jithara (2/20) and the right-arm leg-spin of Limansa Thilakarathna, daughter of former Sri Lanka Captain Tillakaratne Dilshan.

Sri Lanka had no problem in chasing down the moderate target reaching it in the 14th over.

The in-form left-handed opener Sanjana Kavindi with 6 national WT20Is under her belt continued her prolific run with the bat racing to 46 off 27 balls before attempting to sweep a straight ball and falling lbw, 4 short of what would have been her third consecutive half-century.

The win was completed by Limansa (16*) and Umayangana Peiris (1*) after Sri Lanka had suffered back to back run outs of Nethmi Upeksha (16) and Shashini Gimhani (9).

With this win Sri Lanka continued to head the standings with 4 wins from 5 matches and 8 points followed by Bangladesh who have 3 wins and 6 points also from 5 matches. Both Sri Lanka and Bangladesh qualify for the final. Host Pakistan ended up with 1 win and 2 points completing all their 6 matches.

Sri Lanka and Bangladesh will meet in the final league match tomorrow which would virtually be a dress rehearsal for Friday’s final.

Scores: 

Pakistan U19 Women 105-8 (20) (Aqsa 20, Shahar Bano 24*, Yeshali Jithara 2/20, Limansa Thilakarathna 3/14) lose to Sri Lanka U19 Women 106-4 (13.3) (Sanjana Kavindi 46, Nethmi Upeksha 16, Limansa Thilakarathna 16*) by six wickets.

Handshakes after Sri Lanka complete a comprehensive win over Pakistan

title: Bergs stuns Alcaraz in Shanghai as Zverev claims year’s top tennis ranking | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:17
-     - 10

Zizou Bergs

Seven-time Grand Slam champion Carlos Alcaraz has suffered a shock 7-5 7-6(4) defeat by unseeded Belgian Zizou Bergs in the Shanghai Masters round of 32, a result ⁠that also confirmed Alexander Zverev as the ATP’s year-end world number one tennis player.

Fresh from defending his Japan Open title and building momentum after a lengthy wrist injury layoff, Alcaraz never found his rhythm in a scrappy two-hour, two-minute contest on Monday.

The second-seeded Spaniard, who ⁠was sidelined for nearly five months before returning at the US Open in late August and reaching the quarterfinals, joined 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic and US Open runner-up Ben Shelton among the high-profile casualties at the Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) Masters 1000 event.

Bergs produced a composed all-court performance, thriving in the quick conditions as the 27-year-old broke Alcaraz’s serve three times to clinch the ‌biggest victory of his career.

Bergs had lost their only previous meeting, falling to Alcaraz in the last 16 of last year’s Japan Open, but showed no signs of intimidation as he outplayed the 23-year-old in key moments.

“This is something that has been very tough for me,” Bergs said, when asked about getting a win against one of the biggest names on the ATP Tour.

“I often have too much respect for these guys, which is part of my culture and I’m proud of that. But it gets a little bit in the way when you have to ⁠play them…

“The more experience you have practising against them and playing matches, the more it ⁠becomes the new standard a little bit. To have this moment, for me it is a little bit of a relief. I feel like now I really can win against these guys.”

Alcaraz conceded he was below his best.

“I didn’t play the way that I wanted to play. A lot of mistakes. I didn’t find a good position on the return,” Alcaraz said.

“Obviously, credit to him. I would say he served really well.

“But when I got into the rhythm, when I got into the point, I made a lot of mistakes. I wasn’t feeling comfortable with my shots. So, I’m really disappointed with today’s match ⁠because I didn’t find the solution. I just made a lot of unforced errors.”

The upset also guaranteed French Open and US Open champion Zverev, 29, the ATP’s year-end world ⁠number one ranking, making him the first German and the oldest first-time player to achieve the feat.

Zverev’s route to the top spot opened after Italian Jannik Sinner had not played ⁠since beating him in the Wimbledon final on July 12 due to a ⁠knee injury.

The 25-year-old Sinner missed the North American hard-court tournaments, the US Open and the ongoing Asian contests. The five-time major winner will also sit out the European indoor season and the ATP Finals in Turin, where he has lifted the trophy in each of the last two years.

title: Steven Smith doesn’t take the field after blow to the head while batting | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:14
-     - 13

Australia batter Steven Smith was being assessed for concussion on the fourth day of the first Test against South Africa in Durban after a blow to the helmet from Anrich Nortje.

Smith was pinned on the fourth delivery of his innings on Monday, when a bouncer from Nortje took him on the helmet on the fifth ball of the 13th over of Australia’s second innings. The ball ended up flying around to fine leg. As is mandatory, Smith was assessed on the field by the physio and the doctor, while his helmet was changed before he continued his innings. He made 27 off 41 balls before picking out long-on against Simon Harmer.

Smith did not take the field at the start of South Africa’s second innings, with substitute fielder Michael Neser fielding in the cordon. Smith had caught brilliantly on the third day, especially with his two takes at slip from reverse sweeps against Nathan Lyon.

title: Australia set South Africa a target of 421 | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:14
-     - 11

Matt Renshaw

Australia set South Africa a fourth-innings target of 421 in the first Test at Kingsmead, Durban, declaring their second innings on 314 for 6 by tea on day four after Matt Renshaw backed up his first-innings 190 with 82 off 99 balls.

At stumps, South Africa finished the day on 4-102 trailing by 319 runs, requiring 319 more runs to reach a target of 421

Australia scored at 5.41 runs an over, with captain Pat Cummins hitting 32 not out off 12 balls and Beau Webster finishing unbeaten on 39.

Renshaw, batting at No. 5, appeared on course for a second century of the match before he was caught and bowled by spinner Keshav Maharaj, who took the catch low to the ground. Third umpire Richard Illingworth ruled that Maharaj’s fingers were under the ball. Renshaw, who returned to Test cricket as an opener against Bangladesh in August after three and a half years away, is the only batter in the match to have passed 50. He reached his half-century with a reverse-sweep for four off Simon Harmer, a shot he used to good effect throughout.

Australia needed quick runs, as bad light had cut short each of the first three days in the final session, with dark clouds building over Durban as they typically do at this time of year. Resuming on 33 without loss, after only 5.4 overs were possible on day three, Australia got an aggressive start from new opener Nic Maddinson.

Maddinson, a surprise selection who had not played first-class cricket since March 2025, made 48 off 38 balls, a contrast to his 33-ball duck in the first innings. He survived early edges through the slips before driving freely through the off side to pass his previous highest Test score of 22, and hit Harmer for a six down the ground before Anrich Nortje bowled him with a yorker.

Travis Head made 11, edging Marco Jansen to mid-on. Head averages 31.6 in Tests away from home against almost 52 in Australia, and his highest score in his last six innings is 29, raising the question of whether he should swap places with Renshaw and return to No. 5.

Steven Smith was struck on the helmet by a Nortje bouncer but responded with three boundaries and brought up a 50-run partnership with Marnus Labuschagne by hitting Harmer down the ground. He fell soon after, caught by Jansen at the second attempt.

Labuschagne, under pressure after going without a Test century since the 2023 Ashes, looked in good touch at No. 3 but holed out to cover off Maharaj for 37 off 58 balls, an identical score from an identical number of deliveries to his first innings.

The pitch is becoming harder to bat on, with variable bounce and significant turn for Maharaj and Harmer, after South Africa failed to make use of easier conditions on day three. Nortje had several deliveries keep low through to wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, a sign Australia’s fast bowlers will look to exploit.

title: Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Antonelli moves to brink of title | Daily FT
summary:
Tuesday, 13 October 2026 03:11
-     - 9

Lewis Hamilton apologised to his Ferrari team after overriding the pit wall and choosing his own strategy during the Singapore Grand Prix.

Hamilton’s error means Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli is in a position to clinch his first world title at the next race, the US Grand Prix in Austin, after finishing third behind race winner Max Verstappen and Leclerc.

Antonelli’s lead over team-mate George Russell, who finished ninth after starting from the back of the grid, has extended to 102 points and 111 over Hamilton.

The Italian needs to leave Austin with an advantage of at least 125 points to clinch the title, with five races at most remaining after that.

He will do so if he wins the race with Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower at the Circuit of the Americas on 25 October.

If he becomes champion this year, the 20-year-old will be the youngest in Formula 1 history.

Ferrari were on course to finish second and third with Charles Leclerc and Hamilton, but instead the seven-time champion fell back to sixth in the closing laps as he fought a losing battle to hold off three cars while on fading tyres.

Hamilton apologised to the team over the radio on the slowing-down lap after the race, saying: “Sorry, boys. I let you down today with that strategy. My call, and I lost us valuable points. I’ll try and make up for it in the next one.”

Team principal Frederic Vasseur said: “Clearly we asked them to pit. Charles pitted. Lewis didn’t want to pit because he... I don’t know why. And then he realised it was the wrong call. It’s why he apologised to the team.

“Now it’s not a drama for me that he made the wrong call. I’m making mistakes, he’s making mistakes, we’re all making mistakes sometimes. Now we have to look ahead and make mistakes positively.”

Hamilton did not speak to the media after the race after saying he felt unwell and being given permission to miss the interview zone, known as the media pen.

In a statement released by Ferrari, he said: “Under the virtual safety car, the team called me in but I missed the entry. After that, I decided to stay out and try to hold track position to the end but in the closing laps, I was struggling massively with tyre degradation and lost three places, finishing P6, which doesn’t reflect the pace we had in the car.

“A painful lesson, but I take full responsibility for the decisions I made. Not every call will work out, and I can accept getting it wrong but I’m sorry for the team for the points we lost today. They put so much into every weekend, and I wanted to deliver more for them. I’ll continue to put the work in and come back fighting at the next race.”

Ferrari called both cars in to the pits during a virtual safety car that was called mid-race. Stopping under the VSC saves about 10 seconds versus stopping under racing conditions.

Hamilton said in the statement that his decision was based on his improved pace on the soft-compound tyre after he had been forced to make an earlier pit stop than planned because the medium tyre on which he started the race was not performing.

“At a track [where it’s] difficult to overtake, you need to try something different and I chose to start on a new medium tyre, to go long and try to make a one-stop work,” he said.

“Unfortunately the medium didn’t perform as well as the soft. I had a good second stint and the pace was back, but I couldn’t make the progress I needed.”

His first stop was six laps before Leclerc’s and when the Monegasque emerged on to the track, Hamilton was right behind him and initially faster.

At one stage, he pointed out to the team that he had “lost two seconds on that lap”, but the team decided not to invert the cars. Hamilton followed Leclerc within two seconds for a further 10 laps before slowly starting to lose ground a couple of laps before the VSC.

Vasseur said the team decided to leave Leclerc in front because he had pitted later than Hamilton.

“The tyre advantage was for Charles, that he pitted six laps later,” Vasseur said. “I think it was the right call.”

However, that argument appears to be somewhat undermined by the fact that the medium tyre emerged as the worst option for the race - as Hamilton had found out in the first stint and other drivers later discovered.

Leclerc was put back on the soft when he stopped under the VSC.
